entries.52beb09e5873f0e4ff7b83930f1cc46926e89907: Verse 42. Frankly forgave. Freely forgave, or forgave entirely without any compensation. This is not designed to express anything about the way in which God forgives sinners. He forgives-- forgives freely, but it is in connection with the atonement made by the Lord Jesus. If it was a mere debt which we owed to God, he might forgive, as this creditor did, without any equivalent. But it is crime which he forgives. He pardons as a moral governor. A parent might forgive a debt without any equivalent; but he cannot pardon an offending child without regarding his own character as a parent, the truth of his threatenings, the good order of his house, and the maintenance of his authority. So our sins against God, though they are called debts, are called so figuratively. It is not an affair of money, and God cannot forgive us without maintaining his word, the honour of his government, and law--in other words, without an atonement. It is clear that by the creditor here our Saviour meant to designate GOD, and by the debtors, sinners and the woman present. Simon, whose life had been comparatively upright, was denoted by the one that owed fifty pence; the woman, who had been an open and shameless sinner, was represented by the one that owed five hundred. Yet neither could pay. Both must be forgiven or perish. So, however much difference there is among men, all need the pardoning mercy of God, and all, without that, must perish.
entries.64cc55297fe76ae4b130a82af184c1f1ef0525a3:
Verse 43. I suppose, &c. He saw not the point of our Lord's parable. By thus saying, therefore, he condemned himself, and prepared the way for our Lord's reproof.

(f) (rightly judged) Ps 116:16-18, 1Cor 15:9, 1Timm 1:13-16
entries.36c1900b53dbefc112be438ba9e4fd965ec9f462:
Verse 44. Seest thou this woman? You see what this woman has done to me, compared with what you have done. She has shown me expressions of regard which you, in your own house, have not shown.

I entered into thine house. I came at your invitation, where I might expect all the usual rites of hospitality.

Thou gavest me no water for my feet. Among Eastern people it was customary, before eating, to wash the feet; and to do this, or to bring water for it, was one of the rites of hospitality. See Gen 18:4, Jud 19:21. The reasons for this were, that they wore sandals, which covered only the bottom of the feet, and that when they ate they reclined on couches or sofas. It became therefore necessary that the feet should be often washed.
entries.7d19d1315dbacaeef9fd55494359d6c5cdc423fe:
Verse 45. Thou gavest me no kiss. The kiss was a token of affection or a common mode of salutation, and Simon had even neglected this mark or welcoming him to his house. It was often used among men as a sign of salutation. Comp. Gen 33:4, Ex 18:7, Mt 26:49.

Hath not ceased to kiss my feet. How striking the difference between the conduct of Simon and this woman! He, with all the richness of a splendid preparation, had omitted the common marks of regard and affection. She, in humility, had bowed at his feet, had watered them with tears, and had not ceased to kiss them. The most splendid entertainments do not always express the greatest welcome. There may be in such entertainments much insincerity--much seeking of popularity or some other motive; but no such motive could have operated in inducing a broken-hearted sinner to wash the Saviour's feet with tears.
entries.9d96cca1042cb13407e780af0348aae30b343d98:
Verse 46. My head with oil. The custom of pouring oil upon the head was universal among the Jews. The oil used was sweet oil or oil of olives, prepared in such a way as to give an agreeable smell. It was also used to render the hair more smooth and elegant. Ruth 3:3; 2Sam 12:20, 2Sam 14:2, Ps 23:5.

With ointment. This ointment was a mixture of various aromatics, and was therefore far more costly and precious than the oil commonly used for anointing the head. Her conduct, compared with that of Simon, was therefore more striking. He did not give even the common oil for his head used on such occasions. She had applied to his feet a far more precious and valuable unguent. He, therefore, showed comparatively little love. She showed much.

(g) "My head" Ps 23:5.
entries.b552404ee2fdfdafd990cb12cfa93dda70f30395:
Verse 47. Wherefore I say unto thee. As the result of this, or because she has done this; meaning by this that she had given evidence that her sins had been forgiven. The inquiry with Simon was whether it was proper for Jesus to touch her or to allow her to touch him, because she was such a sinner, Lk 7:39. Jesus said, in substance, to Simon,
"Grant that she has been as great a sinner as you affirm,
and even grant that if she had continued so it might be
improper to suffer her to touch me, yet her conduct shows
that her sins have been forgiven. She has evinced so much
love for me as to show that she is no longer such a sinner
as you suppose, and it is not, therefore, improper that she
should be suffered to come near me."
For she loved much. In our translation this would seem to be given as a reason why her sins had been forgiven--that she had loved much before they were pardoned; but this is clearly not the meaning. This would be contrary to the whole New Testament, which supposes that love succeeds, not precedes forgiveness; and which nowhere supposes that sins are forgiven because we love God. It would be also contrary to the design of the Saviour here. It was not to show why her sins had been forgiven, but to show that she had given evidence that they actually had been, and that it was proper, therefore, that she should come near to him and manifest this love. The meaning may be thus expressed:
"That her sins, so many and aggravated, have been
forgiven--that she is no longer such a sinner as you
suppose, is manifest from her conduct. She shows deep
gratitude, penitence, love. Her conduct is the
proper expression of that love. While you have
shown comparatively little evidence that you felt that
your sins were great, and comparatively little
love at their being forgiven, she has shown that
she felt hers to be great, and has loved much."
To whom little is forgiven. He who feels that little has been forgiven--that his sins were not as great as those of others. A man's love to God will be in proportion to the obligation he feels to him for forgiveness. God is to be loved for his perfections, apart from what he has done for us. But still it is proper that our love should be increased by a consideration of his goodness; and they who feel--as Christians do--that they are the chief of sinners,will feel under infinite obligation to love God and their Redeemer, and that no expression of attachment to him can be beyond what is due.
entries.dd2a93c3f049e8d3fa1bf5afd153b86f15e95a4a: Verse 48. Thy sins are forgiven. What a gracious assurance to the weeping, loving, penitent! How that voice, spoken to the troubled sinner, stills his anguish, allays his troubled feelings, and produces peace to the soul! And how manifest is it that he that could say thus must be God! No man has a right to forgive sin. No man can speak peace to the soul, and give assurance that its transgressions are pardoned. Here, then, Jesus gave indubitable proof that he was God as well as man; that he was Lord of the conscience as well as the pitying friend; and that he was as able to read the heart and give peace there, as he was to witness the external expression of sorrow for sin.
entries.bffb29d358c70c44321f952f62b109872e53cccb:
Verse 49. Who is this, &c. A very pertinent question. Who could he be but God? Man could not do it, and there is no wonder that they were amazed.

(h) (Who is this that forgiveth sins.) Mt 9:2,3, Mk 2:7
entries.53812e34d1d76ac932e7d6e8d24f868613eece82:
Verse 50. Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace. Mk 5:34.

(i) "Thy faith" Hab 2:4, Mt 9:22, Mk 5:34, 10:52, Lk 8:48, 18:42, Eph 2:8

entries.f38440076f2d1422b1b10049c12245f676744539: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.5" sID="gen97793" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.5">Luke 7:5</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">For he loveth our nation</hi> This was, no doubt, a commendation given him by the Jews on account of his piety: <note n="501"> <div sID="gen97795" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il n’ y a point de doute que les Juifs recommandent cest homme pour l'affection et le bon zele qu'il avoit a la crainte de Dieu</foreign>.” — “There is no doubt that the Jews recommend this man for the affection and the good zeal which he had for the fear of God.”<div eID="gen97795" type="x-p"/> </note> for his <hi type="italic">love of a nation </hi>universally hated could proceed only from zeal for the Law, and from reverence for God. By <hi type="italic">building a synagogue, </hi>he showed plainly that he favored the doctrine of the Law. The Jews had therefore good grounds for saying that, as a devout worshipper of God, he had claims on Christ for receiving such a favor. They discover, at the same time, a marvellous stupidity in admitting, by their own acknowledgment, that a Gentile possesses that grace of God which they despise and reject. If they consider Christ to be the minister and dispenser of the gifts of God, why do they not receive the grace offered to them before bringing foreigners to enjoy it? But hypocrites never fail to manifest such carelessness and presumption, as not to hesitate to look upon God as under some sort of obligations to them, and to dispose of his grace at their pleasure, as if it were in their own power; and then, when they are satisfied with it, or rather because they do not deign to taste it, they treat it as useless, and leave it to others.<div eID="gen97794" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97793" osisID="Luke.7.5" type="section"/>
entries.352136a6c469f40bad8afb565404d8e043b8d00a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.11" sID="gen97821" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.11">Luke 7:11</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And it happened, that he went into a city.</hi> In all the miracles of Christ, we must attend to the rule which Matthew lays down. We ought to know, therefore, that this young man, whom Christ raised from the dead, is an emblem of the spiritual life which he restores to us. The name of the city contributes to the certainty of the history. The same purpose is served by what Luke says, that <hi type="italic">a great multitude</hi> from every direction followed him: for Christ had many attendants along with him, and many persons accompanied the woman, as a mark of respect, to the interment of her son. The resurrection of the young man was beheld by so many witnesses, that no doubt could be entertained as to its truth. There was the additional circumstance of its being a crowded place: for we know that public assemblies were held at the gates. That the dead man was carried out of the city was in accordance with a very ancient custom among all nations. <hi type="italic">Jerome </hi>says that, in his time, the city of Nain was still in existence, two miles below Mount Tabor, in a southerly direction.<div eID="gen97822" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97821" osisID="Luke.7.11" type="section"/>
entries.60f2112d989b656a803263d3062b1a7345a0c0e1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.12" sID="gen97823" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12. </hi><hi type="italic">The only son of his mother.</hi> The reason which induced Christ to restore the young man to life was, that he saw the <hi type="italic">widow </hi>bereft of her <hi type="italic">only son, </hi>and had compassion on her: for he did not withhold his favor till some one requested it, as he did on other occasions; but anticipated the prayers of all, and <hi type="italic">restored the son to his mother, </hi>by whom nothing of this sort was expected. We have here a striking emblem of his freely bestowed compassion in raising us from death to life. <hi type="italic">By touching the coffin </hi>he intended perhaps to show, that he would by no means shrink from death and the grave, in order to obtain life for us. He not only deigns to touch us with his hand, in order to quicken us when we are dead, but, in order that he might raise us to heaven, himself descends into the grave.<div eID="gen97824" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97823" osisID="Luke.7.12" type="section"/>
entries.ce00da81f4c19f4865f22812c481cb1a9a7d73af: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.14" sID="gen97825" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14. </hi><hi type="italic">Young man, I say to thee.</hi> By this word Christ proved the truth of the saying of Paul, that <hi type="italic">God calleth those things which are not, as they were,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.4.17">Romans 4:17</reference>.) He addresses the dead man, and makes himself be heard, so that death is suddenly changed into life. We have here, in the first place, a striking emblem of the future resurrection, as Ezekiel is commanded to say, <hi type="italic">O ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord,</hi> [<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.37.4">37:4</reference>.] Secondly, we are taught in what manner Christ quickens us spiritually by faith. It is when he infuses into his word a secret power, so that it enters into dead souls, as he himself declares,<div eID="gen97826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97827" type="x-p"/>The hour cometh, when the dead shall hear the voice of <lb/> the Son of God, and they who hear shall live, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.5.25">John 5:25</reference>.)<div eID="gen97827" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97825" osisID="Luke.7.14" type="section"/>
entries.01083bbe98aaec76b145bdc1796fc655e8781023:
16. And fear seized all A sense of the divine presence must have brought fear along with it: but there is a difference between the kinds of fear Unbelievers either tremble and are dismayed; or, struck with alarm, murmur against God: while devout and godly persons, moved by reverence, willingly humble themselves. Fear, therefore, is here taken in a good sense, because they gave the honor which was due to the power of God which they had beheld, and rendered to God not only homage, but thanksgiving.
God hath visited his people I understand this to refer not to every kind of visitation, but to that which would restore them to their original condition. Not only were the affairs of Judea in a depressed state, but they had sunk under a wretched and frightful slavery, as if God were not looking at them. The only remaining hope was, that God had promised to be their Redeemer, after they had endured very heavy calamities. I have no doubt, therefore, that they were excited by the miracle to expect an approaching restoration to prosperity: only they fall into a mistake as to the nature of the visitation Though they acknowledge and celebrate the unwonted grace of God in this respect, that a great Prophet hath risen up among us, yet this eulogium comes very far short of the dignity and glory of the promised Messiah. Hence it appears that the faith of that people was, at this time, exceedingly confused, and involved in many unfounded imaginations.
MATTHEW 8:19-22; LUKE 9:57-62
Matthew 8:19-22
Luke 9:57-62
19. And a scribe approaching said to him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou shalt go. 20. And Jesus saith to him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests: but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head. 21. And another of his disciples said to him, Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father. 22. And Jesus said to him, Follow me, and allow the dead to bury their dead.
57. And it happened, while they were walking in the way, one said to him, I will follow thee withersoever thou shalt go. 58. Jesus said to him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests: but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head. 59. And he said to another, Follow me. And he said, Lord, permit me to go first and bury my father. 60. And Jesus said to him, Allow the dead to bury their dead: but go thou and proclaim the kingdom of God. 61. And another said to him, I will follow thee, Lord, but permit me first to bid farewell to those who are in my house. 62. Jesus said to him, No man who, having put his hand to the plough, shall look back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
entries.6ee4e3395b35f095547bda464361e734c8de53b5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.29" sID="gen98598" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.29">Luke 7:29</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And all the people hearing.</hi> This part is left out by Matthew, though it throws no small light on the connection of the words; for it was this circumstance which gave rise to Christ’s expostulation, when he perceived that the scribes persisted so obstinately in despising God. The substance of this passage is, that the common <hi type="italic">people </hi>and the <hi type="italic">publicans </hi>gave glory to God; while <hi type="italic">the Scribes, </hi>flattering themselves with confidence in their own knowledge, cared little for what Christ said. At first sight, this tends only to obscure, and even to disfigure, the glory of the Gospel, that Christ could not gather disciples to himself, except from the dregs and offscourings of the people; while he was rejected by those who had any reputation for holiness or learning. But the Lord intended, from the beginning, to hold out this example, that neither the men of that age, nor even posterity, might judge of the Gospel by the approbation of men; for we are all by nature inclined to this vice. And yet nothing is more unreasonable than to submit the truth of God to the judgment of <hi type="italic">men, </hi>whose acuteness and sagacity amounts to nothing more than mere vanity. Accordingly, as Paul says, <hi type="italic">“God </hi>hath chosen that part which is weak and foolish in the eyes of the world, that he may cast down from its height whatever appears to be mighty and wise,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.27">1 Corinthians 1:27</reference>.) Our duty is to prefer this <hi type="italic">foolishness of God, </hi>to use Paul’s expression, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.25">1 Corinthians 1:25</reference>,) to all the display of human wisdom.<div eID="gen98599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98600" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Justified God.</hi> This is a very remarkable expression. Those who respectfully embrace the Son of God, and assent to the doctrine which he has brought, are said to ascribe righteousness to God. We need not therefore wonder, if the Holy Spirit everywhere honors faith with remarkable commendations, assigns to it the highest rank in the worship of God, and declares that it is a very acceptable service. For what duty can be deemed more sacred than to vindicate God’s righteousness? The word <hi type="italic">justify </hi>applies generally, no doubt, to every thing connected with the praises of God, and conveys the idea, that God is beheld with approbation, and crowned with glory, by the people who embrace that doctrine of which He is the author. Now, since faith <hi type="italic">justifies </hi>God, it is impossible, on the other hand, but that unbelief must be blasphemy against him, and a disdainful withholding of that praise which is due to his name. This expression also teaches us, that men are never brought into complete subjection to the faith until, disregarding the flesh and sense, they conclude that every thing which comes from God is just and holy, and do not permit themselves to murmur against his word or his works.<div eID="gen98600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98601" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Having been baptized with the baptism of John.</hi> Luke means that the fruits of <hi type="italic">the baptism </hi>which they had received were then beginning to appear; for it was a useful preparation to them for receiving the doctrine of Christ. It was already an evidence of their piety that they presented themselves to be <hi type="italic">baptized. </hi>Our Lord now leads them forward from that slender instruction to a higher degree of progress, as the scribes, in despising the baptism of John, shut against themselves, through their pride, the gate of faith. If, therefore, we desire to rise to full perfection, let us first guard against despising the very least of God’s invitations, <note n="25"> <div sID="gen98602" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Gardons premierement de mespriser un seul moyen par lequel Die nous convie</foreign>;” — “let us first guard against despising a single method by which God invites us.”<div eID="gen98602" type="x-p"/> </note> and be prepared in humility to commence with small and elementary instructions. Secondly, let us endeavor that, if our faith shall have a feeble beginning, it may regularly and gradually increase.<div eID="gen98601" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98598" osisID="Luke.7.29" type="section"/>
entries.ac195d5f62fe75c98e951b8f0a74f8bee909fed0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.30" sID="gen98603" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">Despised the counsel of God within themselves. The counsel of God</hi> is mentioned by way of respect, as contrasted with the wicked pride of the scribes; for the term <hi type="italic">counsel </hi>carries along with it a dignity, which protects the doctrine of God against the contempt of men. Literally, Luke says, that they <hi type="italic">despised </hi>Against Themselves: and indeed I do not disapprove of the meaning which is preferred by some, that the scribes were rebellious to their own destruction. But as Luke’s narrative is simple, and as the preposition <foreign xml:lang="el">εἰς</foreign> is often used in the sense of <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐν</foreign> I have chosen rather to translate it, <hi type="italic">within themselves; </hi>as meaning, that although they did not openly and expressly contradict, yet as they inwardly swelled with hidden pride, they <hi type="italic">despised within themselves</hi><div eID="gen98604" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98603" osisID="Luke.7.30" type="section"/>
entries.0c4466f059a96425f0212618ea77b39ff40b3db2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.31" sID="gen98605" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">To what shall I compare?</hi> He does not include all the men of his age, but speaks particularly of the scribes and their followers. He charges them with this reproach, that while the Lord endeavored, by various methods, to draw them to himself, they repelled his grace with incorrigible obstinacy. He employs a comparison, which was probably taken from a common amusement of children; for there is probability in the conjecture, that the children divided themselves into two bands, and sang in that manner. And, indeed, I think that, in order to abase the pride of the scribes, Christ intentionally borrowed from children the materials of his reproof: thus declaring that, however distinguished they were, nothing more was necessary to condemn them than a song which children were wont to sing in the market-place for their amusement.<div eID="gen98606" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98605" osisID="Luke.7.31" type="section"/>
entries.52571b5ed6f7d1f847060f53fee0dc69ab730a0b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.33" sID="gen98607" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33.</hi> <hi type="italic">For John the Baptist came.</hi> Leading an austere life, he thundered out repentance and severe reproofs, and sung, as it were, a plaintive song; while the Lord endeavored, by a cheerful and sprightly song, to draw them more gently to the Father. Neither of those methods had any success, and what reason could be assigned except their hardened obstinacy? This passage also shows us, why so wide a difference existed, as to outward life, between Christ and the Baptist, though both had the same object in view. Our Lord intended, by this diversity, and by assuming as it were a variety of characters, to convict unbelievers more fully; since, while he yielded and accommodated himself to their manners, he did not bend them to himself. But if the men of that age are deprived of every excuse for repelling, with inveterate malice, a twofold invitation which God had given them, we too are held guilty in their persons; for God leaves not untried any sort of pleasing melody, or of plaintive and harsh music, to draw us to himself, and yet we remain hard as stones. They called John a <hi type="italic">demoniac, </hi>just as persons of unsound mind, or whose brain is disturbed, are usually called <hi type="italic">madmen.</hi><div eID="gen98608" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98607" osisID="Luke.7.33" type="section"/>
entries.a6e4f932d7d21fdacc62e6419a94613d7b3e6be3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.34" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.34" sID="gen98609" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">34.</hi> <hi type="italic">The Son of man came.</hi> To <hi type="italic">eat and drink</hi> means here nothing more than to live in the customary way; as Christ says that John <hi type="italic">came neither eating nor drinking, </hi>because he confined himself to a peculiar diet, and even abstained from ordinary food. This is more fully expressed by the words of Luke, <hi type="italic">neither eating bread nor drinking wine.</hi> Those who think that the highest perfection consists in outward austerity of life, and who pronounce it to be an angelical life when a person is abstemious, <note n="26"> <div sID="gen98611" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand un homme ne boira point de vin</foreign>;” — “when a person will drink no wine.”<div eID="gen98611" type="x-p"/> </note> or mortifies himself by fasting, ought to attend to this passage. On this principle John would rank higher than the Son of God; but, on the contrary, we ought to maintain, that<div eID="gen98610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98612" type="x-p"/>bodily exercise profiteth little, but godliness <lb/> is profitable to all things, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.4.8">1 Timothy 4:8</reference>.)<div eID="gen98612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen98613" type="x-p"/>And yet we must not make this a pretense for giving a loose rein to the flesh, by indulging in luxuries and effeminacy: only we must beware of superstition, lest foolish men, imagining that perfection lies in matters of a purely elementary nature, neglect the spiritual worship of God. Besides, while Christ accommodated himself to the usages of ordinary life, he maintained a sobriety truly divine, and did not encourage the excesses of others by his dissimulation or by his example.<div eID="gen98613" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.34" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98609" osisID="Luke.7.34" type="section"/>
entries.15e26cd3bfcd876cac87ef3117edf694f4aea921:
35. And Wisdom is justified This passage is variously explained by commentators. Some maintain that Wisdom was acquitted by the Jews, because, conscious of guilt, and judges of their own unbelief, they were compelled to acknowledge, that the doctrine which they rejected was good and holy. By the children of Wisdom they understand the Jews who boasted of that title. Others think that it was spoken in irony: “It is in this manner that you approve of the Wisdom of God, of which you boast that you are the children?” But as the Greek preposition ἀπό
“Le mot Grec que nous avons rendu par De;” — “the Greek word which we have translated by.”
does not properly relate to an agent, some explain it, that Wisdom is acquitted by her children, and is no longer under obligation to them, in the same manner as when an inheritance is transferred to another. Thus Paul says, that Christ was justified (δεδικαίωται) from sin, (Romans 6:7,) because the curse of sin had no longer any power over him.
Some interpret it more harshly, and with greater excess of freedom, to mean that Wisdom is estranged from her children But granting that this were the import of the Greek preposition, I look upon the other meaning as more appropriate, that Wisdom, however wickedly she may be slandered by her own sons, loses nothing of her worth or rank, but remains unimpaired. The Jews, and particularly the scribes, gave themselves out as children of the Wisdom of God; and yet, when they trod their mother under their feet, they not only flattered themselves amidst such heinous sacrilege, but desired that Christ should fall by their decision. Christ maintains, on the contrary, that, however wicked and depraved her children may be, Wisdom remains entire, and that the malice of those who wickedly and malignantly slander her takes nothing from her authority.
I have not yet brought forward that meaning which appears to my own mind the most appropriate and natural. First, the words of Christ contain an implied contrast between true children and bastards, who hold but an empty title without the reality; and they amount to this: “Let those who haughtily boast of being the children of Wisdom proceed in their obstinacy: she will, notwithstanding, retain the praise and support of her own children. Accordingly, Luke adds a term of universality, by all her children; which means, that the reluctance of the scribes will not prevent all the elect of God from remaining steadfast in the faith of the Gospel. With respect to the Greek word ἀπό, it undoubtedly has sometimes the same meaning as ὑπό. Not to mention other instances, there is a passage in Luke’s Gospel, (17:25,) where Christ says, that he must suffer many things, καὶ ἀποδοκιμασθὢναι ἀπὸ τὢς γενεᾶς ταύτης, and be rejected By this generation. Everybody will admit, that the form of expression is the same as in the corresponding clause.
“On void bien que la ce mot De se rapporte a la personne qui fait, et non pas a celuy qui souffre;” — “It is very evident that the word By relates to the person that acts, and not to him who suffers.”
Besides, Chrysostom, whose native language was Greek, passes over this matter, as if there were no room for debate. Not only is this meaning more appropriate, but it corresponds to a former clause, in which it was said, that God was justified by the people, (v. 29.) Although many apostates may revolt from the Church of God, yet, among all the elect, who truly belong to the flock, the faith of the Gospel will always remain uninjured.

entries.e2045ae0d7ee8d9638ecbeeb66a42ef2170f4aca: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.36" sID="gen99337" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36.</hi> <hi type="italic">And one of the Pharisees requested him.</hi> This narrative shows the captious disposition, not only to take, but to seek out, offenses, which was manifested by those who did not know the office of Christ. A <hi type="italic">Pharisee</hi> invites Christ; from which we infer, that he was not one of those who furiously and violently opposed, nor of those who haughtily despised his doctrine. But whatever might be his mildness, he is presently offended when he sees Christ bestow a gracious reception on a woman who, in his opinion, ought not to have been permitted to approach or to converse with him; and, accordingly, disowns him as <hi type="italic">a prophet, </hi>because he does not acknowledge him to be the Mediator, whose peculiar office it was to bring miserable sinners into a state of reconciliation with God. It was something, no doubt, to bestow on Christ the honor due to a prophet; but he ought also to have inquired for what purpose he was sent, what he brought, and what commission he had received from the Father. Overlooking the grace of reconciliation, which was the main feature to be looked for in Christ, the Pharisee concluded that he was <hi type="italic">not a prophet</hi> And, certainly, had it not been that through the grace of Christ this woman had obtained the forgiveness of her sins, and a new righteousness, she ought to have been rejected.<div eID="gen99338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99339" type="x-p"/>Simon’s mistake lies only in this: Not considering that Christ came to save what was lost, he rashly concludes that Christ does not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy. That we may not share in this dislike, let us learn, first, that Christ was given as a Deliverer to miserable and lost men, <note n="239"> <div sID="gen99340" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que Christ a este donne pour liberateur au genre humain, miserable et perdu</foreign>;” — “that Christ was given as a deliverer to the human race, miserable and lost.”<div eID="gen99340" type="x-p"/> </note> and to restore them from death to life. Secondly, let every man examine himself and his life, and then we will not wonder that others are admitted along with us, for no one will dare to place himself above others. It is hypocrisy alone that leads men to be careless about themselves, <note n="240"> <div sID="gen99341" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui fait que les hommes se me cognoissent</foreign>;” — “which makes men forget themselves.”<div eID="gen99341" type="x-p"/> </note> and haughtily to despise others.<div eID="gen99339" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99337" osisID="Luke.7.36" type="section"/>
entries.73facf77b0fda961a63317cc89518d564dbb54a5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.37" sID="gen99342" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">A woman who was a sinner</hi> The words stand literally as I have translated them,(<foreign xml:lang="el">ἥτις ἧν ἁμαζτωλὸς</foreign>.)<hi type="italic"> Erasmus </hi>has chosen to take the pluperfect tense, <hi type="italic">who Had Been a sinner,</hi> <note n="241"> <div sID="gen99344" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Quoe fuerat peccatrix</hi></foreign><div eID="gen99344" type="x-p"/> </note> lest any one should suppose that at that time she still <hi type="italic">was a sinner</hi> But by so doing, he departed from the natural meaning; for Luke intended to express the place which the woman held in society, and the opinion universally entertained respecting her. Though her sudden conversion had rendered her a different person in the sight of God from what she had previously been, yet among men the disgrace attaching to her former life had not yet been effaced. She was, therefore, in the general estimation of men <hi type="italic">a sinner, </hi>that is, a woman of wicked and infamous life; and this led <hi type="italic">Simon </hi>to conclude, though erroneously, that Christ had not the Spirit of discernment, since he was unacquainted with that infamy which was generally known. <note n="242"> <div sID="gen99345" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Veu qu’il ne cognoist point l’infamie de la vie de ceste femme qui estoit notoire a un chacun</foreign>;” — “since he does not know the infamy of the life of this woman, which was notorious to every one.”<div eID="gen99345" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99343" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99342" osisID="Luke.7.37" type="section"/>
entries.1e22568589fe64297d2bd04cc633f920637bdba5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.40" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.40" sID="gen99346" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">40.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Jesus answering said.</hi> By this reply Christ shows how egregiously Simon was mistaken. Exposing to public view his silent and concealed thought, he proves himself to possess something more excellent than what belonged to the <hi type="italic">Prophets; </hi>for he does not reply to his words, but refutes the sentiment which he kept hidden within his breast. Nor was it only on Simon’s account that this was done, but in order to assure every one of us, that we have no reason to fear lest any sinner be rejected by him, who not only gives them kind and friendly invitations, but is prepared with equal liberality, and—as we might say—with outstretched arms, to receive them all.<div eID="gen99347" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.40" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99346" osisID="Luke.7.40" type="section"/>
entries.726f1bba5c66a4fe2199bda32b112bf980a726ee: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.41" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.41" sID="gen99348" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">41.</hi> <hi type="italic">A certain creditor had two debtors</hi> The scope of this parable is to demonstrate, that Simon is wrong in condemning the woman who is acquitted by the heavenly judge. He proves that she is righteous, not because she pleased God, but because <hi type="italic">her sins were forgiven; </hi>for otherwise her case would not correspond to the parable, in which Christ expressly states, that the creditor <hi type="italic">freely forgave the debtors who were not able to pay. We </hi>cannot avoid wondering, therefore, that the greater part of commentators have fallen into so gross a blunder as to imagine that this woman, by her <hi type="italic">tears, </hi>and her <hi type="italic">anointing, </hi>and her <hi type="italic">kissing his feet, </hi>deserved the pardon of her sins. The argument which Christ employs was taken, not from the cause, but from the effect; for, until a favor has been received, it cannot awaken gratitude, <note n="243"> <div sID="gen99350" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Veu que le remerciment presuppose tousiours qu’on ait avant receuquelque bien</foreign>;” — “since gratitude always presupposes that some favor has been received.”<div eID="gen99350" type="x-p"/> </note> and the cause of reciprocal love is here declared to be a free forgiveness. In a word, Christ argues from the fruits or effects that follow it, that this woman has been reconciled to God.<div eID="gen99349" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.41" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99348" osisID="Luke.7.41" type="section"/>
entries.07bf86ccce0ae34942b514a059d1ee0279706909: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.44" sID="gen99351" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">44.</hi> <hi type="italic">And turning to the woman.</hi> The Lord appears to compare Simon with the woman, in such a manner as to make him chargeable with nothing more than light offenses. But this is spoken only in the way of concession. “Suppose now, Simon,” he says, “that the guilt from which God discharges thee was light, <note n="244"> <div sID="gen99353" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mettons le cas, Simon, que le fardeau des pechez, desquels Dieu t’a descharge fust petit</foreign>;” — “let us put the case, Simon, that the burden of the sins, from which God has discharged thee, was small.”<div eID="gen99353" type="x-p"/> </note> and that this woman has been guilty of many and very heinous offenses. Yet you see how she proves by the effect that she has obtained pardon. For what mean those profuse tears, those frequent kisses of the feet, that precious ointment? What mean they but to acknowledge, that she had been weighed down by an enormous burden of condemnation? And now she regards the mercy of God with fervor of love proportioned to her conviction that her necessity had been great.”<div eID="gen99352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99354" type="x-p"/>From the words of Christ, therefore, we are not at liberty to infer, that Simon had been a debtor to a small amount, or that he was absolved from guilt. <note n="245"> <div sID="gen99355" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et s’il avoit este absous de la condamnation qu’il avoit encourue</foreign>;” —”and if he had been absolved from the condemnation which he had incurred.”<div eID="gen99355" type="x-p"/> </note> It is more probable that, as he was a blind hypocrite, he was still plunged in the filth of his sins. But Christ insists on this single point, that, however wicked the woman may have been, she gave undoubted proofs of her righteousness, by leaving no kind of duty undone to testify her gratitude, and by acknowledging, in every possible way, her vast obligations to God. At the same time, Christ reminds Simon, that he has no right to flatter himself, as if he were free from all blame; for that he too needed mercy; and that if even he does not obtain the favor of God without pardon, he ought to look upon this woman’s gifts, whatever might have been her former sins, as evidences of repentance and gratitude.<div eID="gen99354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99356" type="x-p"/>We must attend to the points of contrast, in which the woman is preferred to Simon. She <hi type="italic">moistened his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head; </hi>while <hi type="italic">he </hi>did not even order <hi type="italic">water </hi>to be given, according to custom. She <hi type="italic">did not cease to kiss his feet, </hi>while <hi type="italic">he </hi>did not deign to receive Christ with the kiss of hospitality. <note n="246"> <div sID="gen99357" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En lieu que l’autre n’a pas mesme daigne le baiser par une facon commune de civilite</foreign>;” — “whereas the other did not even deign to kiss him, according to an ordinary custom of civility.”<div eID="gen99357" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">She </hi>poured precious<hi type="italic"> ointment on his feet, </hi>while <hi type="italic">he </hi>did not even <hi type="italic">anoint his head with oil.</hi> But why did our Lord, who was a model of frugality and economy, permit the expense of the <hi type="italic">ointment? </hi>It was because, in this way, the wretched sinner testified that she owed all to him. He had no desire of such luxuries, was not gratified by the sweet odor, and did not approve of gaudy dress. But he looked only at her extraordinary zeal to testify her repentance, which is also held out to us by Luke as an example; for her sorrow, which is the commencement of repentance, was proved by her tears. By placing herself <hi type="italic">at Christ’s feet behind him, </hi>and there lying on the ground, she discovered her modesty and humility. By the <hi type="italic">ointment, </hi>she declared that she offered, as a sacrifice to Christ, herself and all that she possessed. Every one of these things it is our duty to imitate; but the pouring of the <hi type="italic">ointment </hi>was an extraordinary act, which it would be improper to consider as a rule. <note n="247"> <div sID="gen99358" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A este un acte special et extraordinaire, duquel si on vouloit faire une reigle generale, ce seroit un abus</foreign>;” — “was a special and extraordinary act, of which, if we wished to make a general rule, it would be a mistake.”<div eID="gen99358" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99356" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99351" osisID="Luke.7.44" type="section"/>
entries.3ba6ce42adec00171b3b2d4ded9cf43250c37448: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.47" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.47" sID="gen99359" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">47.</hi> <hi type="italic">Her many sins are forgiven</hi> Some interpret the verb differently, <hi type="italic">may her many sins be forgiven,</hi> and bring out the following meaning: — “As this woman evinces by remarkable actions, that she is full of ardent love to Christ, it would be improper for the Church to act harshly and severely towards her; but, on the contrary, she ought to be treated with gentleness, whatever may have been the aggravations of her offenses.” But as <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀφέωνται</foreign> is used, in accordance with the Athic dialect, for <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀφεῖνται</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>we must dispense with that subtlety of exposition which is disapproved by the context; for a little after, Christ uses the same words in his address to the woman, where the imperative mood would not apply. Here, too is added a corresponding clause, that <hi type="italic">he to whom less is forgiven loveth less</hi><div eID="gen99360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99361" type="x-p"/>The verb, which is in the present tense, must, no doubt, be resolved into a preterite. <note n="248"> <div sID="gen99362" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Combien qu’il faut resoudre le verbe du temps present en un temps passe: comme quand il dit, <hi type="italic">Ses pechez luy sont pardonnez: </hi>il faut entendre, <hi type="italic">Ont este pardonnez</hi></foreign>;” — “though the verb must be resolved from the present tense into a past tense: as when he says, <hi type="italic">Her sins are forgiven, </hi>we must understand it to mean, <hi type="italic">Have been forgiven.</hi>”<div eID="gen99362" type="x-p"/> </note> From the eager desire which she had manifested to discharge all the duties of piety, Christ infers that, although this woman might have been guilty of many sins, the mercy of God was so abundant towards her, that she ought no longer to be regarded as a sinner. Again, <hi type="italic">loving </hi>is not here said to be the cause of pardon, <note n="249"> <div sID="gen99363" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il n’est pas dit ici que la dilection ou amour des hommes envers Dieu soit la cause de la remission des pechez</foreign>;” — “it is not here said that the <hi type="italic">loving, </hi>or the love of men towards God, is the cause of the forgiveness of sins.”<div eID="gen99363" type="x-p"/> </note> but a subsequent manifestation, as I have formerly mentioned; for the meaning of the words is this: — “They who perceive the display of deep piety in the woman form an erroneous judgment, if they do not conclude that God is already reconciled to her;” so that the free pardon of sins comes first in order. Christ does not inquire at what price men may purchase the favor of God, but argues that God has already forgiven this wretched sinner, and that, therefore, a mortal man ought not to treat her with severity.<div eID="gen99361" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.47" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99359" osisID="Luke.7.47" type="section"/>
entries.0d88436ad894f703814158668b5a163b0fd38e5b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.48" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.48" sID="gen99364" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">48.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven.</hi> It may be asked, why does Christ now promise to her the pardon which she had obtained, and of which she had been assured? Some reply that these words were uttered, not so much on her own account, as for the sake of others. For my own part, I have no doubt that it was chiefly on her own account; and this appears more clearly from the words that follow. Nor ought we to wonder, that the voice of Christ again pronounces an absolution of the woman, who had already tasted his grace, and who was even convinced that he was her only refuge of salvation. Thus, at the present day, faith is previously necessary, when we pray that the Lord would forgive our sins; and yet this is not a useless or superfluous prayer, but the object of it is, that the heavenly Judge may more and more seal his mercy on our hearts, and in this manner may give us peace. Though this woman had brought with her a confident reliance on that grace which she had obtained, yet this promise was not superfluous, but contributed greatly to the confirmation of her faith.<div eID="gen99365" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.48" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99364" osisID="Luke.7.48" type="section"/>
entries.ff4de392d9f42899583e5f95af3c20d39934ca42: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.49" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.7.49" sID="gen99366" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">49.</hi> <hi type="italic">And those who sat at table with him began to say within themselves.</hi> Hence we again learn, that ignorance of Christ’s office constantly leads men to conceive new grounds of offense. The root of the evil is, that no one examines his own wretched condition, which undoubtedly would arouse every man to seek a remedy. There is no reason to wonder that hypocrites, who slumber amidst their vices, <note n="250"> <div sID="gen99368" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui se plaisent et fiattent en leurs vices</foreign>;” — “who please and flatter themselves amidst their vices.”<div eID="gen99368" type="x-p"/> </note> should murmur at it as a thing new and unexpected, when Christ forgives sins.<div eID="gen99367" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.7.49" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99366" osisID="Luke.7.49" type="section"/>

50. Thy faith hath saved thee. To repress those murmurings,
“Pour reprimer les murmures de ces gens;” — “to repress the murmurings of those people.”
and, at the same time, to confirm the woman, Christ commends her faith. Let others grumble as they may, but do thou adhere steadfastly to that faith which has brought thee an undoubted salvation.
“Qui t’a apporte certitude de salut;” — “which has brought thee certainty of salvation.”
At the same time, Christ claims for himself the authority which had been given to him by the Father; for, as he possesses the power of healing, to him faith is properly directed. And this intimates that the woman was not led by rashness or mistake to come to him, but that, through the guidance of the Spirit, she had preserved the straight road of faith. Hence it follows, that we cannot believe in any other than the Son of God, without considering that person to have the disposal of life and death. If the true reason for believing in Christ be, that God hath given him authority to forgive sins, whenever faith is rendered to another, that honor which is due to Christ must of necessity be taken from him. This saying refutes also the error of those who imagine that the forgiveness of sins is purchased by charity; for Christ lays down a quite different method, which is, that we embrace by faith the offered mercy. The last clause, Go in peace, denotes that inestimable fruit of faith which is so frequently commended in Scripture. It brings peace and joy to the consciences, and prevents them from being driven hither and thither by uneasiness and alarm.

               <ns0:p n="11">11 And it came to pass the day after, that he went into a city called Nain, and many of his disciples went with him, and much people.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and much people of the city was with her.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And he came and touched the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>coffin.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> biere and they that bare him stood still, And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 9.40.</ns0:note> Arise.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And he that was dead, sat up, and began to speak, And he delivered him to his mother.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> alone gives us an account of this Miracle of our Saviours. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentioneth only the raising from the dead of <ns0:hi>Iairus</ns0:hi> his Daughter. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> addeth this, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> adds that of <ns0:hi>Lazarus, Iohn</ns0:hi> 11. by which our Lord did mightily shew his Divine Po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer, and gave us some <ns0:hi>first Fruits</ns0:hi> of the more general Resur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection, as well as declared himself to be, as he elsewhere saith, the <ns0:hi>Resurrection</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Life.</ns0:hi> The place where this Miracle was done, was called <ns0:hi>Naim.</ns0:hi> H. <ns0:hi>Stephen Heb. Cald. Gr. et Lat. nomina,</ns0:hi> &c. tells us, it was a City or Town about two Miles from <ns0:hi>Mount Tabor,</ns0:hi> at the Foot of the lesser Mount <ns0:hi>Hermon,</ns0:hi> near to <ns0:hi>Hendor.</ns0:hi> It was the Custom of the Jews to bury their Dead without their Cities. Christ met this Dead Body carry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing out. He was it seems her only Child, and she was a Widow, so under a great Affliction, God by this Providence having <ns0:hi>quench<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the only Coal, she had left in</ns0:hi> Israel. <ns0:hi>And when the Lord saw her</ns0:hi> (the Text saith) <ns0:hi>he had Compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not.</ns0:hi> None moved him on the behalf of the Widow, neither do we read, that she her self spake to him. Only our Saviour's Bowels were moved at the sight of her Sorrow, and consideration of her loss. It is observable that our Saviour wrought his <ns0:hi>healing Miracles,</ns0:hi> 1. Sometimes at the motion, and desire of the Parties to be healed, 2. Sometimes, at the desires of others on their behalf. 3. Sometimes of his own free motion, neither themselves nor others Solliciting him for any such Act of Mercy toward them, and that in the three first Miracles (of which <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> giveth us an account here, and <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.) which he wrought after his famous Sermon on the Mountain, he gave us an instance of all these, in his healing of the <ns0:hi>Leper</ns0:hi> Perso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nally beseeching him, of the Centurions Servant at the Intreaty of the Elders of the Jews, and of the Widows Son here, upon his sight of the Womans Affliction, none Solliciting him. Thereby shewing us that we ought not to stay our Hand from doing good, when we have proper objects and opportunities before us, until we be importuned, and Sollicited, thereunto. Christ saying to her, <ns0:hi>Weep not,</ns0:hi> forbad not the Natural expression of her Passion, but signifyed a suddain, and not expected Resurrection, so as she should not <ns0:hi>Weep without Hope.</ns0:hi> This said he cometh, and toucheth the <ns0:hi>Bier</ns0:hi> or the Coffin, and saith not, Young Man! <ns0:hi>In the Name of God I say unto thee Arise,</ns0:hi> but, <ns0:hi>Young Man I say unto thee Arise.</ns0:hi> Thereby declaring to them (would they have understood it) that he was the <ns0:hi>Son of God,</ns0:hi> and while he was on Earth, had a power, in, and from himself by the Word of his Mouth to Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand the Dead to Arise. His Word was effective and to evidence it, it is said, That he who was Dead <ns0:hi>sate up,</ns0:hi> so as all might take notice of the Miracle, and <ns0:hi>began to speak. And he delivered him to his Mother.</ns0:hi> To let him know, his Duty to be subject to her, and the Jurisdiction she had over him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And there came a fear on all, and they glorify<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed God, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 24.19. Joh. 4.19: <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 9.17.</ns0:note> That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And this rumour of him went forth through<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out all Judea, and throughout all the region round about.<ns0:note place="bottom">The People here saw the Divine Power, manifestly exerted; for the Keys of the Clouds, the Womb, and the Grave are three Keys, which their Teachers had taught them were kept in Gods Hand alone. All Sense of the <ns0:hi>Divine Presence</ns0:hi> Naturally fills us with fear. Some even the worst of Men, are filled with a stupid fear of Astonishment and Amazement. Pious Persons, or those that are inclined to Piety, are filled with a Fear of <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verence,</ns0:hi> such a <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> we read of, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.65. such was this For it issued in a predication of the Name of God, and a giving to him <ns0:hi>Praise, and Glory.</ns0:hi> For that a <ns0:hi>Great Prophet was risen a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst them,</ns0:hi> thus far God Blessed this <ns0:hi>Miracle</ns0:hi> to make them look upon Christ as a <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> a Great <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> and to look up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on Gods Act in his sending him as an Act of great kindness to the Jews, for that is here plainly understood by them, saying, <ns0:hi>God hath visited his People,</ns0:hi> as before, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.68. and this Ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mour was spead abroad all that Country.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And the disciples of John shewed him of all these things.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And John calling unto him two of his disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples, sent <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> unto Jesus, saying, Art thou he that should come, or look we for another?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 When the men were come unto him, they said, John Baptist hath sent us unto thee, saying, Art thou he that should come, or look we for ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And in that same hour he cured many of <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> infirmities, and plagues, and of evil spirits, and unto many that were blind he gave sight.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Then Jesus answering, said unto them, Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 35.5.</ns0:note> how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are rai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, to the poor the gospel is preached.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And blessed is he whosoever shall not be offen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded in me.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.2, 3, 4, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And when the messengers of John were depar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, he began to speak unto the people concerning John, What went ye out into the wilderness for to see? A reed shaken with the wind?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But what went ye out for to see? A man cloth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in soft rayment? Behold they which are gorgeous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings courts.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and much more than a prophet.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 This is he of whom it is written, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 3.1.</ns0:note> Behold I send my messenger before thy face, which shall pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare thy way before thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 For I say unto ye, Amongst those that are born of women, there is not a greater prophet then John the Baptist, but he that is least in the kingdom of God, is greater then he.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.7, 8, 9. where we met with this Testimony concerning <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> given by our Saviour with some considerable enlargements.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And all the people that heard <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and the publicanes justifyed God, being baptized with the baptisme of John.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 But the Pharisees and lawyers <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>frustra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> rejected <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 20.27.</ns0:note> the counsel of God <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>within themselves.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> against themselves, being not baptized of him.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath not this Addition to our Saviours Commenda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> but it is of great use to introduce our Saviours following Discourse. The Evangelist here divideth the hearers into two sorts. The first were the <ns0:hi>Common People,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Publicanes,</ns0:hi> the former were despised by the Jewish <ns0:hi>Doctors,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rabbies,</ns0:hi> as a Rude Illiterate sort of People, the latter as a Notoriously wicked sort. The second sort were the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> and the Lawyers; of the former, he saith, that they <ns0:hi>being Baptized with the Baptisme of</ns0:hi> John, <ns0:hi>Iustified God,</ns0:hi> that is, they owned, and Publickly declared, and Predicated the Goodness, and Justice ofGod, they approved of what God had done, and Blessed his Name for sending amongst them such a Prophet as <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was, they owned and received him, and were Baptized by him. Whoso believeth the message which God sendeth, and obeyeth it, he <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>stifyeth God,</ns0:hi> he that doth not, <ns0:hi>Accuseth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Condemneth</ns0:hi> God, see <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 3.33. 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.10. <ns0:hi>But the Pharisees and the Law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yers,</ns0:hi> that is<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> not the Scribes of the People, (they were<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but <ns0:hi>Actuaries,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Publick Notaries,</ns0:hi>) but the <ns0:hi>Scribes of the Law,</ns0:hi> whose Office it was to Interpret, and give the Sense of the Law. These <ns0:hi>rejected,</ns0:hi> the Word sometimes signifies to <ns0:hi>despise, Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.8. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.28. sometimes to <ns0:hi>disan<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>l,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.15. sometimes to <ns0:hi>reject,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 7.9. <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 6.26. It is here Interpreted by those Words. <ns0:hi>Not being Bap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tized of him.</ns0:hi> We must understand the Sense of <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> by considering what is here meant by <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the Counsel of God, which some will understand concerning the Purpose of God within himself. Others concerning his <ns0:hi>Revealed Will</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> his Counsel as revealed to us. The matter seemeth to me, but a s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>fe about a Word, which is sometimes taken in one Sense, some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times in another. The Will of God is but <ns0:hi>one,</ns0:hi> only as every one of us keep some part of our mind to our selves, and reveal other parts of it to our Servants, and Children<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> So God who hath Determined and Willed all Events, concealeth some part of it from his Creatures, and Revealeth another part of it to them. It is the Will of God, that this, and that, and the other Person <ns0:hi>should Believe, and be saved.</ns0:hi> He Revealeth as to this, thus much of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>is Will, that <ns0:hi>whoso Believeth, shall be Saved,</ns0:hi> but for that other part of his Will, that this, and that, or the other Man shall Believe, this he concealeth, till he gives them a <ns0:hi>Power to Believe,</ns0:hi> and to receive the Gospel, and then his Will in this particular is <ns0:hi>Revealed.</ns0:hi> Supposing then we here understand by <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Gods <ns0:hi>secret purpose to be understood,</ns0:hi> how is it proved that it must be understood, of his <ns0:hi>secret purposefor their Salvation?</ns0:hi> why should it not be understood of the secret Purpose and Counsel of God, <ns0:hi>to give them the means of Life and Salvation</ns0:hi>? God from all Eternity purposed to give the Jews the Ministry of <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist and Christ,</ns0:hi> as means for their Salvation, not which should be certainly effective of it, but that should have such a Tenden<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy towards it, as without their own refusing, and opposing them it should have been effective, and was in their own Nature a proper mean in order to it: they reject, and refuse it; by this they rejected the Counsel of God, the effect of his Counsel, and so judged themselves unworthy of Eternal Life, by neglecting, despising, and rejecting the use of that means, which was the Product of an Eternal Purpose to send them such means. This Counsel of God is said to be <ns0:hi>rejected</ns0:hi> towards, or against them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves; take it as <ns0:hi>Gods Act,</ns0:hi> it was <ns0:hi>towards themselves,</ns0:hi> that is, for their Good; if we refer it to <ns0:hi>their Act</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Rejection,</ns0:hi> or re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fusal it was <ns0:hi>against themselves,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>judging of themselves un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />worthy of Eternal Life.</ns0:hi> We cannot in this place Translate it <ns0:hi>Disanul,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Frustrate,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Galath.</ns0:hi> 3.15. understanding it as to the <ns0:hi>Divine Act,</ns0:hi> for who can Frustrate or Disanul the Will or Purpose of Man, as to an Act of his own, within his Power to pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> tho indeed as to the <ns0:hi>Event</ns0:hi> it may be <ns0:hi>Disanulled</ns0:hi> as to any good effect as to another, if it be made to depend upon the Action of another. Besides, what need any further Explication of this Phrase, of <ns0:hi>Rejecting the Counsel of God against them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves,</ns0:hi> than what followeth, <ns0:hi>Being not Baptized of him,</ns0:hi> that is, not receiving <ns0:hi>Iohns</ns0:hi> Doctrine of <ns0:hi>Repentance, for the Remis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of Sins,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>bringing forth Fruits worthy of amendment of Life,</ns0:hi> nor submitting to <ns0:hi>Baptisme</ns0:hi> as a Testimony of such <ns0:hi>Repentance</ns0:hi>; for the <ns0:hi>Baptisme</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> in Scripture signifyeth his whole Administration, the Doctrine he Preached, as well as the Ordinance of Baptisme by him Administred, and so must be Interpreted, where our Saviour ask'd the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> whether <ns0:hi>Iohns Baptisme</ns0:hi> was from <ns0:hi>Earth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>from Heaven,</ns0:hi> and they durst not say from Heaven, lest Christ should have ask't them, Why then they <ns0:hi>Believed</ns0:hi> him not? They were not <ns0:hi>Baptized</ns0:hi> of him, is the same thing with, They would be none of his Disciples.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:304" />31 And the Lord said, Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation? and to what are they like.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 They are like unto children sitting in the market-place, and calling one to another, and saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced, we have mourned to you, and ye have not wept.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 3.4. Mark 21.6.</ns0:note> John the Baptist came neither eating bread, nor drinking wine; and ye say, He hath a devil.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 The son of man is come eating and drinking, and ye say, Behold, a gluttonous man, and a wine-bibber, a friend of publicanes and sinners.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 But wisdom is justified of all her children.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.16, 17. where we have this smart Reflection upon the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and the Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerality of the Jews. They were neither pleased full nor fasting, but censorious of the different manner of living of <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> and Christ. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> shewed a more austere and severe Humour, and lived like a <ns0:hi>Recluse,</ns0:hi> you had nothing else to say, you said, <ns0:hi>He had a Devil.</ns0:hi> I have chosen not a less Innocent, but a more free Converse with Men of all sorts, and eat, and drink as other Men, of me you say that I am a <ns0:hi>Wine-bibber,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Glutton,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Friend of Publicanes and Sinners.</ns0:hi> Such was their perverseness, that pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeded from their Enmity to the Doctrine of John and Christ.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 26.6. Mar. 14.3.</ns0:note> And one of the Pharisees desired him that he would eat with him. And he went into the Phari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />see's house, and sate down to meat.<ns0:note place="bottom">This was no small Civility from a <ns0:hi>Pharisee,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were of all others in the Generality of them, the most desperate, and implacable Enemies of our Saviour. But God hath his number amongst all Nations, and all sorts and orders of Men. Our Saviour as was said before, was of a free, and open Converse, and never refused any opportunity offered him to do good. We may soberly Eat, and Drink with Sinners pursuing such De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signs.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And behold a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sate at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster-box of ointment.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> with the ointment.<ns0:note place="bottom">What hath made any Interpreters imagine this was the same Story which is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14. and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 12.2, 3. I cannot tell. The Histories agree scarce in any thing, unless in the bringing the Alabaster-Box of Oyntment, and the Anoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing our Saviour's Feet, whereas there was nothing in those Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tries more ordinary. That Anointing was done in <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in two Miles of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> this in <ns0:hi>Galilee.</ns0:hi> That in the House of one <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Leper,</ns0:hi> this in the House of one <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risee.</ns0:hi> That, a little, this a great while, before our Saviours Passi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. At that <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> was offended, at this <ns0:hi>Simon the Pharisee</ns0:hi> was offended. There Christ Vindicates the Woman from one head of Argument, here from another. Questionless this is ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther quite different piece of History. <ns0:hi>And behold a Woman in the City which was a Sinner.</ns0:hi> That is, a remarkable Sinner, it is a Word generally so used, and applyed to Women, signifies a <ns0:hi>Prostitute,</ns0:hi> or at least one of an ill Report as to Chastity; <ns0:hi>was,</ns0:hi> referreth here to the time past, tho lately past, she had lately been infamous and notorious, but it appeareth by what fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loweth, that she was not so now, otherwise than in the Opinion, and Vogue of the People; according to whose opinion, tho uncha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritable enough, <ns0:hi>Quae semel fuit mala, semper praesumitur esse mala in eodem genere mali,</ns0:hi> a Person who hath once been bad is always presumed so to be, through their ignorance of the Power of Divine Grace in changing the Heart, or their Malice against and Envy towards, those whose Hearts they see so chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged. But whatever this Woman had been, it seems God had affected her Heart with the Word which Christ had Preached, and filled it with the pure Love of God and Christ, instead of its former fulness of impure Love, and made her Sins as bitter, as they had been formerly pleasant to her. She hearing Christ was Eating Meat at the House of <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Pharisee,</ns0:hi> makes no noise, but cometh <ns0:hi>behind him,</ns0:hi> bringing an <ns0:hi>Alabaster-Box of Ointment, And stood at his Feet behind him, Weeping, and Washing his Feet with her Tears, and wiped them with the Hairs of her Head, Kissed his Feet, and Anointed them with Oyntment.</ns0:hi> Weeping in the Sense of her Sins, and so plentiful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, as she washed the Feet of Christ with her Tears, spoke a broken and a Contrite Heart. <ns0:hi>Wiping them with her Hair,</ns0:hi> her <ns0:hi>Hair</ns0:hi> with which she had offended through Wantonness, Plait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing it, and Adorning her self by the dress of it to allure her Lovers; she now useth to testify her Abhorrence of her former Courses, and <ns0:hi>Kissed his Feet and Anointed them with the Oint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Kiss</ns0:hi> is a <ns0:hi>Symbol</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> and not of Love only, but of Subjection and Worship; by this she both shewed her Love to Christ, and also her Subjection to him, she Kissed Christ in the <ns0:hi>Psalmists</ns0:hi> Sence, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2.11. It was not a Kiss of Love only, but of Reverence and Subjection, like <ns0:hi>Iosephs Kiss to Iacob, Gen.</ns0:hi> 50.2. <ns0:hi>Moses his Kiss to Iethro, Exod.</ns0:hi> 18.7. nay of the <ns0:hi>Highest Reverence,</ns0:hi> for such was the <ns0:hi>Kiss of the Feet.</ns0:hi> And to testify her <ns0:hi>Adoration</ns0:hi> of him. Thus the Idola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters <ns0:hi>Kissed the Calves, Hos.</ns0:hi> 13.2. and <ns0:hi>Baal,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 19.28. washing and anointing with <ns0:hi>Oyl,</ns0:hi> was a common Comple<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment they used in those Countries, for Cleansing, and Cooling thefeet; she had been a great Sinner, she now shews the profoundest Sorrow, greatest Love, Humility, Subjection, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But some may say, <ns0:hi>How could she come behind him, sitting at Meat and do this,</ns0:hi> while we sit at Meat our Feet are before us? This confirmeth the Notion I mentioned before, in my Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.20. concerning the Jewish <ns0:hi>manner of sitting at Meat,</ns0:hi> which was <ns0:hi>Kneeling</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>resting thei<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Bodies upon their Legs leaning backwards</ns0:hi>; admitting that all that we here read of this Woman, was very easie; for his Legs being thrust out backward, the Soles of his Feet were turned up, and she might with convenience enough, come at them, behind him to wash, and to wipe and to ano<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>nt them, which it is hard to conceive how she could do, adm<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tting him to have sate, as we do, puting our feet forward under the Table.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:304" />39 Now when the Pharisee which had bidden him, saw <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> he spake within himself, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.2.</ns0:note> This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman <ns0:hi>this is,</ns0:hi> that toucheth him, for she is a sinner.<ns0:note place="bottom">How easily are persons, (tho seemingly well inclined and fair,) offended, who have not the Love of God rooted and grounded in their hearts? Did then all Men who were Prophets, know Persons at first sight? It is certain they knew no more of Peoples hearts and Lives, then God was pleased to reveal to them or they knew by converse with them, and observation of them. 2, Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose she had been a Sinner, might she not be a convert now; and did not her behaviour toward Christ, (before mentioned) witness a change in her? 3. Admit she had been yet such a Sinner, yet might not she touch Christ? This was indeed a Pharisaical error That all not of their own Religion, and all Persons notorious for some Sins, were in the same order, as <ns0:hi>Lepers,</ns0:hi> and other Persons that were <ns0:hi>Levitically,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Legally Vnclean,</ns0:hi> so as none might touch them, but that contact made them also Unclean. It is said, also of the <ns0:hi>Samaritans,</ns0:hi> that when they meet a <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>Christian,</ns0:hi> they would first call out to him, <ns0:hi>Do not touch me.</ns0:hi> That there was of old such a Party amongst the Jews that cryed, <ns0:hi>stand by thy self, come not near to me, for I am holier then thou,</ns0:hi> is plain from <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 65. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
